title: P0 hostedapi dedicated fallback driver memory leak retrospective
summary: On 2029-07-22 we experienced a P0 degradation of the Hosted API: a sustained p98/p99 latency spike and an increase in 5xx for streaming endpoints. Root cause was a regression in a GPU driver update rolled to a subset of Dedicated fallback nodes: the driver leaked pinned GPU host memory over multi-hour windows, causing worker eviction and TCP session stalls that cascaded into the hosted control plane routing fallback and client-facing failures.
impact: From 2029-07-22 15:12 UTC to 2029-07-22 18:03 UTC: ~43% of streaming sessions experienced stalls or 5xx; non-streaming generation p95 increased from 220ms to 1.8s; short-term SLO burn and escalations from 11 customers. No customer data was exposed; requests were either delayed or failed.
detection: Alerting fired for node memory pressure (node.mem.gpuhost_pinned > threshold), followed by increased worker restarts and SYN/TCP retransmits on fallback pool. On-call noticed rising client complaints in #prod-ops and increased 5xx alert on hostedapi-streaming-5xx. SRE pager triggered at 15:25 UTC; initial hypothesis: memory leak on Dedicated fallback nodes.
timeline:
2029-07-22 14:50 UTC - control plane rollout started: driver v525.12 staged to 30% of Dedicated fallback nodes
2029-07-22 15:10 UTC - first memory-pressure anomaly on pool-fallback-us-east-1
2029-07-22 15:20 UTC - streaming 5xx surge detected, SRE pager
2029-07-22 15:35 UTC - operator attached to node, saw cgmanager OOMs and dmesg showing pinned host allocations
2029-07-22 16:00 UTC - mitigation: roll driver to previous version on impacted nodes and cordon+drain affected hosts
2029-07-22 16:45 UTC - routed fallback off to ephemeral pool to relieve pressure; service latency began falling
2029-07-22 17:10 UTC - all impacted nodes rolled back; memory usage stabilized
2029-07-22 18:03 UTC - post-incident observation window passed; alerts quieted and customer communications sent.
root_cause: A GPU driver update (v525.12) introduced a regression in pinned memory accounting for host-visible allocations used by the CUDA runtime on inference processes. Over time (hours) the driver failed to release pinned host allocations during process teardown, causing total host memory reserved for pinned buffers to climb until worker evacuation and kernel-level stalls triggered TCP write and poll stalls. The control plane's fallback policy began routing more traffic to the Dedicated fallback pool (capacity-preserving behavior), which amplified the impacted surface and exposed hosted API clients to higher latencies and 5xx.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Rollback GPU driver on impacted Dedicated fallback hosts to v525.09. 2) Cordon + drain impacted hosts to force worker restarts on healthy nodes. 3) Temporarily disable automatic fallback routing to Dedicated pool (control-plane flag) and route to ephemeral pool. 4) Increase retention of short-lived hostmetrics to detect pinned memory earlier. 5) Open vendor ticket with GPU driver vendor describing pinned host memory leak with dmesg logs and reproduction notes.
postmortem_analysis: Why cascade happened: the combination of (a) driver leak that grew slowly and (b) fallback routing that concentrated load on the Dedicated fallback pool created a positive feedback loop. Metrics that were slow to show failure mode (pinned host allocation) meant the system relied on worker restarts and CPU OOMs to reveal the issue, by which point client-impact was significant. Our test staging missed the leak because the preflight used 30-minute soak tests; the leak requires multi-hour churn under realistic request patterns to surface.
longterm_actions:
- Add a long-duration GPU driver soak test in staging (6+ hours) with production-like streaming workloads
- Improve monitoring: expose pinned-host-memory metric from nodes and alert at earlier thresholds
- Add control-plane guardrail: do not route >40% ephemeral stream traffic to fallback pools without manual confirmation
- Automate busy-drain: when worker restarts > threshold due to memory pressure, immediately stop new allocations and rotate node out
- Coordinate with infra vendor to get a driver patch; add driver version gating in rollout orchestration
- Post-deployment verification step: run a 2-hour pipeline that tracks pinned memory delta per node
- Update incident runbook with pinned-memory investigation checklist and commands
runbook_draft:
(Draft runbook section - pinned GPU host memory event)
1) Surface: check node metric node.mem.gpuhost_pinned and node.restarts in Graphite/Dash
2) If pinned_mem > 2GB sustained for 30m: cordon node and run sudo dmesg | grep -i pinned or sudo journalctl -k | grep -i pin to capture kernel messages
3) Run: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data then monitor worker restarts on target node
4) Rollback driver: use infra-driver-orch rollback --pool <pool> --version v525.09 (if safe to do)
5) If rollback unavailable: toggle control-plane flag fallback.enable=false and shift traffic to ephemeral pool; call infra on-call to schedule immediate host replacement
6) Collect logs: /var/log/syslog, /var/log/dmesg, and inference worker logs for 2 hours post-action for vendor ticket
7) Post-action: keep node cordoned for 4 hours; once pinned_mem delta is stable, uncordon
oncall_notes:
- Initial operator action that helped: cordon+drain of first affected node reduced local retransmits and bought time for rollback.
- Be cautious with automatic fallback: the platform-level safeguard permitted high concentration of traffic to Dedicated fallback — plan to reduce aggressiveness until we have pinned-memory metrics.
- Commands that were helpful: 
  - kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels | grep fallback
  - /opt/infra/bin/driver-check --node <node-id> --version
  - sudo journalctl -k -u systemd -n 200 | grep -i pinned
- Communication: pager channel to #prod-ops + #gcs (GTM) for customer comms; Security=yes (no data exposure).
- Post-incident Slack TL;DR to customers: brief explanation of root cause, mitigation, and timeline.
